title: Pyare Lal Bhargava v. State of Rajasthan
summary: A government superintendent removed official files, had them copied, and returned them. The Supreme Court held this was theft, ruling that theft does not require permanent deprivation — any unauthorised moving of property out of a person's possession, causing even temporary loss, suffices.
principle: Even temporary dishonest removal of movable property amounts to theft; permanent deprivation is not required.

title: Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
summary: The accused inflicted a single fatal spear wound. The Supreme Court laid down the four-part test for murder under the 'thirdly' clause: a bodily injury must be present, its nature proved, that very injury intended (not accidental), and the injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
principle: For murder by intentional bodily injury, the injury must be both intended and sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

title: K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra
summary: A naval officer shot his wife's paramour. The Supreme Court applied the exception of grave and sudden provocation, holding the provocation must be both grave and sudden with no time for passion to cool; a killing after a cooling-off period is murder, not culpable homicide.
principle: Grave and sudden provocation reduces murder to culpable homicide only if there was no time for passion to cool.

title: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
summary: Upholding the constitutional validity of the death penalty, the Supreme Court held that life imprisonment is the rule and the death sentence an exception, to be imposed only in the 'rarest of rare' cases where the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
principle: The death penalty may be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases where life imprisonment is inadequate.

title: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
summary: Building on Bachan Singh, the Supreme Court laid down guidelines for identifying the 'rarest of rare' case, weighing factors such as the manner, motive, magnitude and victim of the crime, and requiring a balance of aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
principle: 'Rarest of rare' is assessed by balancing aggravating and mitigating circumstances under settled guidelines.

title: Mahadeo Prasad v. State of West Bengal
summary: The Supreme Court held that to constitute cheating, a dishonest or fraudulent intention must exist at the very time of the inducement that leads the victim to part with property; a mere later failure to pay is not cheating.
principle: Cheating requires dishonest intention at the time of inducement, not merely a subsequent breach.

title: Rashmi Kumar v. Mahesh Kumar Bhada
summary: The Supreme Court set out the ingredients of criminal breach of trust: entrustment of property (or dominion over it) and dishonest misappropriation or conversion by the person entrusted. Entrustment is essential to the offence.
principle: Criminal breach of trust requires entrustment of property followed by its dishonest misappropriation.

title: S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar
summary: The Supreme Court distinguished criminal breach of trust from cheating: breach of trust turns on entrustment and later misappropriation, whereas cheating turns on a dishonest inducement existing from the outset. A mere breach of contract is neither.
principle: Breach of trust hinges on entrustment; cheating on dishonest inducement from the start — a contractual breach alone is neither.

title: Kans Raj v. State of Punjab
summary: In a dowry-death matter, the Supreme Court cautioned that while the husband may be liable, in-laws and other relatives cannot be roped in automatically; specific overt acts against each accused must be proved beyond reasonable doubt to avoid over-implication.
principle: In dowry-death cases, relatives cannot be implicated without specific proof of their individual role.

title: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
summary: The Supreme Court held that the contents of an electronic record can be proved only as secondary electronic evidence and are admissible only when accompanied by the certificate required under Section 65B(4) of the Evidence Act; oral testimony cannot substitute for that certificate.
principle: Secondary electronic evidence is admissible only with the statutory certificate (s.65B(4) Evidence Act; cf. s.63 BSA).

title: Pakala Narayana Swami v. King Emperor
summary: The Privy Council defined 'confession', holding that a confession must either admit the offence in terms or substantially admit all the facts that constitute it; an admission of a single incriminating fact is not by itself a confession.
principle: A confession must admit the offence or substantially all facts constituting it, not merely an incriminating fact.

title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
summary: Acting on reports of custodial deaths, the Supreme Court laid down binding safeguards for every arrest and detention — including an arrest memo attested by a witness, informing a relative of the arrest, and medical examination — to curb custodial abuse.
principle: Arrest and detention must follow mandatory safeguards (arrest memo, intimation to kin, medical exam) against custodial abuse.

title: Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P.
summary: The Supreme Court held that arrest is not automatic on a mere allegation; a police officer must justify the necessity of arrest beyond bare suspicion, and lesser measures such as a notice to appear should be preferred where possible.
principle: Arrest must be justified by necessity, not made routinely on mere allegation or suspicion.

title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
summary: Addressing misuse of arrest powers (notably in Section 498A cases), the Supreme Court directed that for offences punishable up to seven years, police must not arrest automatically but record reasons under the arrest-necessity checklist before making an arrest.
principle: For offences punishable up to seven years, arrest must not be automatic; the necessity must be recorded first.

title: Sanjay Chandra v. CBI
summary: In a serious economic-offence (2G) bail matter, the Supreme Court held that bail should not be refused merely because the allegations are grave; pre-trial detention must not be punitive, and personal liberty under Article 21 must be balanced against securing the trial.
principle: Bail is the rule even in serious economic offences; pre-trial detention must not become punishment.

title: Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P.
summary: A Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence, with a preliminary inquiry permitted only in limited categories; police cannot refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence.
principle: Registration of an FIR is mandatory once information discloses a cognizable offence.
